symbols.name: K
symbols.def: A fixed number of arms that does not vary with \(n\).

symbols.name: \mathcal A_K
symbols.def: \(\mathcal A_K=\{1,\ldots,K\}\).

symbols.name: n
symbols.def: Number of experimental units.

symbols.name: i
symbols.def: Generic unit label.

symbols.name: a
symbols.def: Generic treatment-arm label.

symbols.name: c
symbols.def: Fixed coefficient vector \(c=(c_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\).

symbols.name: S_c
symbols.def: \(S_c=\{a\in\mathcal A_K:c_a\ne0\}\).

symbols.name: L_c
symbols.def: \(L_c=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|c_a|\).

symbols.name: q^\star
symbols.def: \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) for \(a\in S_c\) and \(q_a^\star=0\) otherwise.

symbols.name: t
symbols.def: Generic vector \(t=(t_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\) of arm-specific binary potential outcomes.

symbols.name: \mathcal T_K
symbols.def: \(\mathcal T_K=\{0,1\}^{\mathcal A_K}\), with \(|\mathcal T_K|=2^K\).

symbols.name: z
symbols.def: \(z=(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\), where each labeled unit response type \(t_i=(t_{i,a})_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\) belongs to \(\mathcal T_K\).

symbols.name: Y_i(a)
symbols.def: \(Y_i(a)=t_{i,a}\), the arm \(a\) coordinate of unit \(i\)'s response type in \(z\).

symbols.name: A
symbols.def: \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is drawn from a design selected before the fixed potential outcomes are revealed.

symbols.name: \mathcal D
symbols.def: Probability law of \(A\), chosen without knowledge of the response schedule.

symbols.name: Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
symbols.def: \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(A_i)\).

symbols.name: \tau_c(z)
symbols.def: \(\tau_c(z)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_{i,a}\).

symbols.name: \widehat\tau
symbols.def: Any measurable, possibly biased function of \((A_i,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})_{i=1}^n\), clipped to the range of \(\tau_c(z)\).

symbols.name: R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)
symbols.def: \(R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[(\widehat\tau-\tau_c(z))^2]\), where the expectation is only over assignment from \(\mathcal D\).

symbols.name: \rho_n(c)
symbols.def: \(\rho_n(c)=\inf_{\mathcal D,\widehat\tau}\max_{z\in\mathcal T_K^n}R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)\).

symbols.name: m
symbols.def: For a labeled schedule \(z\), \(m=(m_t)_{t\in\mathcal T_K}\) is its unit-permutation orbit, with \(m_t=\#\{i:t_i=t\}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal M_{n,K}
symbols.def: \(\mathcal M_{n,K}=\{m\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal T_K}:\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_K}m_t=n\}\).

symbols.name: \tau_c(m)
symbols.type: orbit form of the causal contrast
symbols.def: \(\tau_c(m)=n^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_K}m_t\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_a\).

symbols.name: r
symbols.def: \(r=(r_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\), where \(r_a=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal R_{n,K}
symbols.def: \(\mathcal R_{n,K}=\{r\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal A_K}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}r_a=n\}\).

symbols.name: x
symbols.def: \(x=(x_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\), where \(x_a=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{A_i=a,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=1\}\).

symbols.name: h
symbols.def: \(h=(h_{t,a})\) records how many units of response type \(t\) are assigned arm \(a\).

symbols.name: \mathcal H(m,r,x)
symbols.def: The set of \(h\) satisfying \(\sum_a h_{t,a}=m_t\), \(\sum_t h_{t,a}=r_a\), and \(\sum_{t:t_a=1}h_{t,a}=x_a\) for every \(t\) and \(a\).

symbols.name: P_m(x\mid r)
symbols.def: Probability of observed success counts \(x\) under uniform assignment conditional on allocation counts \(r\) and response-type counts \(m\).

symbols.name: \pi
symbols.def: \(\pi=(\pi_r)_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}}\) selects an allocation count and then assigns units uniformly conditional on that count.

symbols.name: \delta
symbols.def: Deterministic estimator based only on the allocation and observed-success orbits \((r,x)\).

symbols.name: G_n(c)
symbols.def: Minimax value of the explicit orbit experiment over \(\pi\), \(\delta\), and \(m\).

symbols.name: p_+
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(p_+=m_{(1,0)}\).

symbols.name: p_-
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(p_-=m_{(0,1)}\).

symbols.name: r_0
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(r_0=m_{(0,0)}+m_{(1,1)}\), with \(p_++p_-+r_0=n\). This aggregation does not replace the separate counts \(m_{(0,0)}\) and \(m_{(1,1)}\) in the orbit likelihood.

symbols.name: X_2
symbols.def: The scalar observation \(X_2=p_++\operatorname{Binomial}(r_0,1/2)\) in the published two-arm reduced experiment.

symbols.name: C_A
symbols.def: The published scalar Airy ground-state constant \(C_A=1.617\ldots\).

symbols.name: \widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star
symbols.def: Under independent assignment supported on \(S_c\) with probabilities \(q^\star\), \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star=\operatorname{proj}_{[-L_c/2,L_c/2]}\!\left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1/2)/q_a^\star\right]\).

symbols.name: a_n
symbols.def: A deterministic positive sequence indexed by \(n\).

symbols.name: C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)
symbols.def: Conditional on the branch in which a normalizer \(a_n\) exists and \(a_nd_n(c)\) converges to a finite positive limit, \(C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_nd_n(c)\).

symbols.name: \sigma
symbols.def: A generic bijection of the arm index set.

symbols.name: \mathfrak G_c
symbols.def: \(\mathfrak G_c=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal A_K):\exists s\in\{-1,1\},\ c_{\sigma(a)}=s c_a\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal A_K\}\).

symbols.name: \rho_n^\dagger
symbols.def: \(\rho_n^\dagger=\rho_n(c^\dagger)\), for which \(C_0(c^\dagger)=1\).

symbols.name: M
symbols.def: Positive integer controlling the mesh of the rational action grid.

symbols.name: j
symbols.def: Generic integer index for the rational action grid.

symbols.name: g
symbols.def: Generic estimator action in the rational grid.

symbols.name: u
symbols.def: Upper bound on every response-type risk in the grid-action LP.

symbols.name: w_{r,x,g}
symbols.def: Nonnegative joint weight for allocation orbit \(r\), observation orbit \(x\), and randomized grid action \(g\).

symbols.name: \Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger
symbols.def: Value of the finite rational linear program that uses the exact three-arm orbit likelihood and permits randomized estimator actions in \(\Gamma_M\).

definitions.name: Signed contrast stabilizer
definitions.construction: \[\mathfrak G_c=\left\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal A_K):\exists s\in\{-1,1\}\text{ such that }c_{\sigma(a)}=s c_a\text{ for all }a\in\mathcal A_K\right\}.\]

definitions.name: Contrast-weighted first-order procedure
definitions.construction: Assign each \(A_i\) independently on \(S_c\) with \(\Pr(A_i=a)=q_a^\star\), and report \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star=\operatorname{proj}_{[-L_c/2,L_c/2]}\!\left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1/2)/q_a^\star\right]\).

definitions.name: Three-arm exact-rational grid-action LP
definitions.construction: For \(K=3\) and \(c=c^\dagger\), minimize \(u\) over rational variables \(\pi_r\ge0\) and \(w_{r,x,g}\ge0\), subject to \(\sum_r\pi_r=1\), \(\sum_{g\in\Gamma_M}w_{r,x,g}=\pi_r\) for every \((r,x)\), and \(\sum_{r,x,g}P_m(x\mid r)w_{r,x,g}\{g-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2\le u\) for every \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,3}\); its value is \(\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\).

definitions.name: Active-face boundary-layer handle
definitions.construction: Starting from the exact orbit game, enumerate binding response-type and allocation faces, expand the discrete risk by a vector Stein identity within each stratum, use the certified \(c^\dagger\) LP sequence to select the normalizer, and pass the primal and dual games to a stratified diffusion-control or spectral value problem with face and corner compatibility conditions.

definitions.name: Contrast-score feedback and converse handle
definitions.construction: Begin with the vector of centered arm scores generated by \(q^\star\); derive an orbit-saddle posterior mean or feedback correction from the limiting value function, lift that correction to finite \(n\), and discretize the squared ground state or dual occupation measure into a least-favorable prior on response-type counts.

statements.statement: For every fixed \(n\), \(K\ge2\), and contrast \(c\), begin with nature choosing a complete labeled schedule \(z\in\mathcal T_K^n\), an arbitrary assignment law \(\mathcal D\), and an arbitrary estimator \(\widehat\tau\). Averaging a procedure over common permutations of unit labels is lossless, and the symmetrized risk is constant on each unit-permutation orbit of schedules. Consequently, with \(m_t=\#\{i:t_i=t\}\), \(\tau_c(z)=\tau_c(m)\), and the labeled minimax risk equals the explicit orbit game: \(\rho_n(c)=G_n(c)\). A symmetrized design is exactly a mixture \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal R_{n,K})\) of uniform assignments conditional on \(r\), and a nonrandomized invariant estimator is \(\delta(r,x)\). The compact convex game admits a minimax procedure and a least-favorable prior on \(\mathcal M_{n,K}\) forming a saddle point.
statements.justification: This theorem converts an unrestricted and exponentially presented experimental decision problem into an explicit finite object that supports computation, asymptotics, and a matched converse.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 1--3, proof of Theorem 2, and Sections 5--6) obtain their scalar two-arm reduction from a least-favorable prior and transformed variables \(S_i\) that are ancillary for the design under that prior. Hull (2026, Theorem 1, proof Steps 1--3) instead averages independent per-unit swaps of the two potential-outcome coordinates together with assignment-bit exclusive-or, and then averages over unit labels. Neither route supplies the fixed-contrast \(2^K\)-type orbit likelihood or a lossless multi-arm saddle point.
statements.consumer: The exact game supplies the finite benchmark needed to audit joint design and analysis choices for a four-arm binary endpoint such as ACTG 175.

statements.statement: The exact response-type game is a strict domain extension of the published two-arm scalar minimax theorem. As an explicitly non-novel sanity and regression clause, when \(K=2\) and \(c=(1,-1)\), this proposal's orbit experiment retains the four distinct counts \(m_{(0,0)},m_{(0,1)},m_{(1,0)},m_{(1,1)}\) in the likelihood \(P_m(x\mid r)\). In particular, no aggregation by individual-effect class is asserted to identify that likelihood kernel. Instead, composing the exact equality \(\rho_n(c)=G_n(c)\) with Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen's published two-arm minimax theorem (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and Section 6) recovers at the minimax-value level their scalar value based on \(X_2=p_++\operatorname{Binomial}(r_0,1/2)\) for estimating \((p_+-p_-)/n\), where \(p_++p_-+r_0=n\). Consequently, \(C_0(c)=1\) and \(d_n(c)=C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), with \(C_A\) determined by the published scalar Airy ground-state problem. For every fixed \(K\ge3\) and every nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\), the same theorem additionally proves equality of the unrestricted labeled-schedule risk and the explicit joint \(2^K\)-response-type orbit game, including arbitrary assignment dependence and possibly biased estimators; those \(K\ge3\) cases are outside the published two-arm theorem. This statement does not assert that the multi-arm game is scalar-nonrepresentable.
statements.justification: The strict-extension result fixes the published binary minimax value as a regression target without collapsing the four-count orbit likelihood, and isolates the new labeled-schedule and orbit-game equality for every fixed multi-arm contrast.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and Section 6) prove the scalar binary minimax value only for two arms; the strict extension is the exact unrestricted equality for \(K\ge3\), not the already published scalar value or Airy expansion.
statements.consumer: It lets the three-arm rational diagnostic and the four-arm ACTG 175 analysis inherit a verified unrestricted decision problem while preserving the published binary game as a regression case.

statements.statement: If \(\mathfrak G_c\) acts transitively on \(S_c\), then \(|c_a|\) is constant over \(a\in S_c\), and the numbers of positive and negative active coefficients are equal. For \(K=3\) and \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), \(\mathfrak G_{c^\dagger}\) has exactly the two arm orbits \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\). Therefore a quotient based solely on signed contrast-preserving arm relabelings cannot merge arm \(1\) with arms \(2\) and \(3\) in the \(c^\dagger\) orbit game. This is an independent orbit diagnostic and not a claim about Hull's coordinatewise swap construction or about scalar representations in general.
statements.justification: The proposition determines exactly which ordinary arm-label symmetries may be used to compress the three-arm diagnostic without changing its contrast.
statements.gap: Bai (2023, Theorem 2.1 and Remark 2.2) shows how invariance can reduce a decision problem, but does not calculate the signed contrast stabilizer or its orbits for the fixed multi-arm response-type game.
statements.consumer: It tells the exact-orbit computation that arms \(2\) and \(3\) may be pooled by symmetry while arm \(1\) must retain a separate allocation label.

statements.statement: Under fixed \(K\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}n\rho_n(c)=C_0(c)=\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|c_a|\right)^2.\] Independent assignment supported on \(S_c\) with \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) and the projected rule \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star\) satisfies \(\max_{z\in\mathcal T_K^n}R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star;z)\le C_0(c)/n\). Because every target \(\tau_c(z)\) lies in \([-L_c/2,L_c/2]\), projection onto this interval cannot increase pointwise squared loss, so \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star\) belongs to the same minimax estimator action space. Conversely, every sequence of randomized designs and possibly biased estimators has asymptotic worst-case labeled-schedule risk at least \(C_0(c)/n+o(n^{-1})\).
statements.justification: It certifies the best robustness constant and the allocation rule before the genuinely nonclassical finite-sample correction is studied.
statements.gap: Bai (2023) derives Neyman allocation for linear procedures under a different superpopulation adversary, while the two 2026 papers prove unrestricted minimaxity only for two arms.
statements.consumer: For ACTG 175, it gives the worst-case allocation benchmark for a prespecified regimen-versus-average contrast rather than default equal allocation.

statements.statement: For \(K=3\), \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), and every \(n,M\ge1\), the grid-action program defining \(\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\) is a finite linear program with rational coefficients and \[\rho_n^\dagger\le\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\le\rho_n^\dagger+\frac{2}{M}+\frac{1}{M^2}.\] Consequently, choosing \(M=n^2\) yields exact-rational primal and dual certificates whose discretization error is \(o(n^{-4/3})\), so the sequence \(n^{4/3}\{n^{-1}-\Lambda_{n,n^2}^\dagger\}\) is a valid early diagnostic for, but not an assumption of, the \(4/3\) exponent. The LP retains the all-zero and all-one response types and every response-type count vector in \(\mathcal M_{n,3}\).
statements.justification: The proposition turns small-\(n\) numerics into certified falsification evidence with an error smaller than the published two-arm second-order scale.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Appendix A and Section 3) study a scalar finite program and its numerical scaling, while Hull (2026, Theorem 1) resolves a two-arm endpoint game analytically; no cited work gives a rational multi-arm orbit LP hierarchy or an error bracket to the unrestricted continuous-action game.
statements.consumer: The diagnostic prevents a long simplex-PDE analysis from proceeding under an incorrect exponent or a falsely multidimensional value.

statements.statement: Using the active-face boundary-layer handle, first determine whether there exists a regularly varying normalizer \(a_n\to\infty\) for which \(a_nd_n(c)\) converges to a finite positive limit. In that existence branch, define \(C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_nd_n(c)\in(0,\infty)\). In the alternative branch, prove that no regularly varying normalization has a finite positive limit and identify the correct, possibly non-regular, asymptotic behavior. Characterize the corresponding limiting value problem and its unique admissible solution, deciding whether simultaneous simplex faces and corners produce a genuinely multidimensional free-boundary Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman problem, an elliptic cone spectral problem, or a separable collection of scalar layers. For \(c=c^\dagger\), the decision must agree with the certified LP scaling and must replace rather than assume the candidate \(a_n=n^{4/3}\) if the certificates disagree.
statements.justification: The normalization and continuum operator are the irreducibly new content: first-order optimality cannot distinguish procedures whose moderate-sample risks differ materially.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026) derive a scalar Airy layer, while Levit (1986) treats smooth elliptic operators; neither covers stratified response-type and allocation corners.
statements.consumer: The answer determines how much finite-sample minimax improvement is available for three- and four-arm binary trials and whether a scalar correction is defensible.

statements.statement: Using the contrast-score feedback and converse handle, construct a finite-\(n\) multi-arm procedure and a least-favorable prior sequence whose upper and lower risks match at the normalization selected by the preceding second-order frontier. Decide whether independent assignment with \(q^\star\) remains second-order optimal; if it does, derive the required multivariate nonlinear shrinkage rule, and if it does not, characterize the necessary finite-\(n\) design correction and certify its improvement in the exact orbit game.
statements.justification: A continuum constant is operationally meaningful only when an implementable design--estimator pair and an unrestricted converse attain the same correction.
statements.gap: Rosenman and Hunter (2026) supply Gaussian multi-arm shrinkage geometry without a fixed-population minimax certificate; Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen's posterior-mean construction is scalar and two-arm.
statements.consumer: The resulting rule gives a prespecified analysis for contrasts among ACTG 175's four regimens with a certified worst-case risk benchmark.

sampling_model.design: An arbitrary probability law \(\mathcal D\in\Delta(\mathcal A_K^n)\) chosen before observing the fixed response schedule; the proposed first-order design assigns units independently with probabilities \(q^\star\).
sampling_model.units: A fixed finite population of \(n\) units with no sampling draw.
sampling_model.treatment: Each unit receives exactly one arm in \(\mathcal A_K\).
sampling_model.potential_outcomes: The binary array \((Y_i(a))_{i,a}\) is fixed; assignment is the only randomness.
sampling_model.overlap: Arms in \(S_c\) have positive probability under \(q^\star\); zero-coefficient arms are irrelevant to \(\tau_c(z)\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: None; nature first chooses the complete labeled schedule \(z\), and \(m\) appears only as its unit-permutation orbit after symmetrization.
sampling_model.loss: Design-based squared error for the finite-population contrast \(\tau_c(z)\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: For two-arm binary SATE, unrestricted minimax risk equals the published scalar reduced game.
For two bounded-outcome arms, independent randomization and a nonlinear endpoint-derived estimator attain unrestricted minimax mean squared error.
Under permutation invariance, complete randomization is minimax, and Neyman allocation with difference-in-means is optimal in the stated linear-estimator model.
Second-order asymptotic optimality is characterized through positive solutions and spectral behavior of a problem-specific Schrödinger operator.
Heteroscedastic Stein-like shrinkage can reduce Gaussian joint squared-error risk for several treatment-versus-control estimates.

tldr: For a fixed multi-arm binary trial and a prespecified scalar contrast, the root contribution starts from the unrestricted game over complete labeled response schedules and proves its exact equality to a finite zero-sum orbit game on \(2^K\) response-type counts. This is a strict \(K\ge3\) domain extension of the published two-arm scalar theorem and yields the projected contrast-weighted first-order saddle rule with \(q_a^\star\propto|c_a|\) and constant \(C_0=(\sum_a|c_a|)^2/4\). A signed-contrast proposition separately records the valid arm-label quotient for \(c=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\); it makes no claim about Hull's coordinatewise swap construction. The open core asks whether a regularly varying second-order normalization with a finite positive limit exists and what active-face geometry governs either branch, while a certified rational LP hierarchy kills incorrect scaling or separability claims before analysis proceeds. A further open question asks for an attaining multi-arm nonlinear rule and a matched least-favorable-prior converse for contrasts such as the four-arm ACTG 175 consumer. In the \(K=2\) sanity clause, the orbit game retains all four response-type counts; only its minimax value is equated to the published scalar binomial value, from which the non-novel \(n^{-4/3}\) Airy expansion follows.

project_justification.gap: Sharp unrestricted binary minimax theory is confined to two arms. Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen obtain scalarization from a least-favorable prior and transformed variables \(S_i\) that are ancillary for the design under that prior. Hull instead averages independent per-unit potential-outcome-coordinate swaps together with assignment-bit exclusive-or, followed by unit averaging. General-contrast design results restrict the estimator or change the adversary, and the second-order literature does not address simultaneous faces and corners of a response-type simplex.
project_justification.niche: For a fixed \(K\)-arm contrast, the unrestricted primitive game is over complete labeled response schedules. Unit-permutation symmetrization can convert that game into an explicit \(2^K\)-response-type orbit game, while the signed contrast stabilizer provides only an independent, precisely scoped arm-label quotient for computation.
project_justification.fill: The project proves the labeled-game-to-orbit-game equality as a strict \(K\ge3\) extension of the published binary scalar theorem, derives the projected first-order saddle rule, records the exact signed arm-label orbits for \(c^\dagger\), and gives a three-arm rational LP approximation with a theorem-level error bracket. It leaves the existence of a regularly varying second-order scale, the corresponding stratified continuum value problem, and a matched implementable multivariate rule and converse as explicit open questions.

related_work: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2, the proof of Theorem 2.2, and Sections 5--6) obtain the two-arm reduction through a least-favorable prior and transformed variables \(S_i\) that are ancillary for the design under that prior; finite minimax duality, a discrete Stein expansion, and a squared-ground-state prior then yield the scalar Airy theory. Their published scalar minimax value and \(n^{-4/3}\) expansion are a method ancestor and a non-novel value-level regression check. This proposal's \(K=2\) orbit likelihood continues to index all four counts \(m_{(0,0)},m_{(0,1)},m_{(1,0)},m_{(1,1)}\); equality with the published scalar result is asserted only after composing minimax-value theorems, not by identifying likelihood kernels through effect-class aggregation. The exact labeled-schedule and orbit-game equality for every fixed \(K\ge3\) is the strict extension. Hull (2026, Theorem 1, proof Steps 1--3, and Section 4) follows a distinct route: independent per-unit swaps of the two potential-outcome coordinates are coupled with assignment-bit exclusive-or and then followed by unit averaging; separate convexity extends the endpoint rule to bounded outcomes. The signed-stabilizer proposition is an independent calculation about ordinary arm relabelings and is not presented as an obstruction to Hull's swap action. Bai (2023) establishes why group invariance can select randomization and derives Neyman allocation in a linear framework; it does not settle the present fixed-schedule arbitrary-estimator value. Levit (1986) supplies the spectral language for converting a second-order risk correction into a principal operator problem, while leaving the stratified simplex geometry untreated. Rosenman and Hunter (2026) motivate borrowing information across arm scores through multivariate shrinkage, but their Gaussian superpopulation risk identity is used only as a construction donor. Mukerjee, Dasgupta, and Rubin (2018) provide the general multiple-treatment finite-population contrast framework. Hammer et al. (1996) provide the applied consumer rather than a theorem comparator: ACTG 175 randomized four regimens and makes a regimen-versus-average binary endpoint contrast operationally meaningful.
technical_internal_limitation: The exact continuous-action squared-loss game is a finite convex quadratically constrained program, not a literal finite LP. The object called an LP in the computational rung is therefore a rational grid-action hierarchy with a proved approximation bracket. Any claim that exact small-\(n\) squared-loss minimax values are obtained by one finite rational LP without this discretization or an additional lossless reformulation would be inaccurate.
honest_scope: The labeled-schedule-to-orbit-game equality, its strict \(K\ge3\) scope extension, the projected first-order saddle rule and constant, the signed arm-orbit calculation, and the rational LP approximation are theorem-level claims. The signed calculation licenses only quotients by signed contrast-preserving arm relabelings; it says nothing about Hull's coordinatewise swap action and does not prove that the multi-arm value is nonseparable or that no scalar statistic exists. Whether any regularly varying normalization has a finite positive second-order limit is open; the constant \(C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)\) is defined only in that existence branch. The second-order scale, operator type, uniqueness theory, and second-order optimality of \(q^\star\) remain genuinely open. The project must stop the multidimensional Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman route if the certified \(c^\dagger\) values separate into scalar games, and it must replace \(n^{4/3}\) if the diagnostic scaling disagrees. For \(K=2\) and \(c=(1,-1)\), all four response-type counts remain in the orbit likelihood. The published scalar binomial value and Airy correction enter only through a non-novel minimax-value regression clause and are not claimed to identify that likelihood kernel.
